reasons: Opinion: 'Under the private search doctrine, the Fourth Amendment is not implicated where the government does not conduct the search itself, but only receives and utilizes information uncovered by a search conducted by a private party.'

Opinion applies this to Microsoft's PhotoDNA hash-match and Detective Ilse's warrantless viewing, concluding 'the government effectively learned nothing from Detective Ilse's viewing of the files that it had not already learned from the private search ... the government did not violate Reddick's Fourth Amendment rights' — the full holding is supported.

Reddick is a Fifth Circuit private-search-doctrine decision resolving a hash-match viewing question; the opinion contrasts the Tenth Circuit's more privacy-protective Ackerman approach, supporting a 'Private and Foreign Searches — Key — hash-match split (5th Cir.)' classification.
residual_risks: The disclosed opinion frames the divergence as the Tenth Circuit (Ackerman, then-Judge Gorsuch) and states no other circuit had confronted the precise question, so 'split' is closer to a doctrinal tension; the page's Treatment prose attributes divergence to the 'Ninth Circuit,' which the disclosed evidence does not support — but that sentence is body prose outside this assertion's payload.
